topics.title: Server Components vs Client Components — what actually differs?
topics.html:
Server ComponentClient Component
RunsOn the server, at request or build timeServer (SSR pass) + browser (hydration)
Ships JS to browserNo — only the rendered outputYes — component + its imports
State / effects / event handlersNoYes
Can await data directlyYes — const data = await db.query()Via use()/React Query/fetch in effect
Access to secrets, DB, fsYesNever
// Server Component (default in the App Router) — no "use client"
export default async function OrdersPage() {
  const orders = await db.orders.findMany();   // runs on the server only
  return <OrdersTable orders={orders} />;      // props must be serializable
}

// Client Component — opts this subtree into the browser bundle
"use client";
export function OrdersTable({ orders }: { orders: Order[] }) {
  const [sort, setSort] = useState<SortKey>("date");
  ...
}
  • "use client" marks a boundary, not a file: everything imported below it becomes client code too. Put it as deep in the tree as possible.
  • Props crossing the boundary must be serializable — no functions, no class instances, no Dates in older setups. You can pass a Server Component as children to a client one; that's the standard escape hatch.
  • The win is bundle size: a heavy markdown or date library used only in a server component ships zero bytes to the browser.
  • Common trap: adding "use client" at the top of a layout, which turns the whole app back into a client app and deletes the benefit.
💬 Say it like this

Server components run only on the server and never send their JavaScript to the browser. They can await data directly, but they cannot have state or event handlers. Client components are the React we always wrote. "use client" is a boundary: everything imported below it goes into the client bundle, so I put it as deep in the tree as possible — usually on a small interactive part like a sort control, not on the whole page.

The practical benefit is bundle size and simpler code: the data fetching sits next to the component that needs it, and heavy libraries stay on the server.

How do you use context with RSC?
Context only works in client components. The usual pattern is a thin client Providers component rendered inside the server root layout.
Do server components replace React Query?
For initial page data, largely yes. For client-side interactive data — polling, infinite scroll, optimistic mutations, cross-screen cache — React Query still wins. Many apps use both: server-render the first payload, hydrate it into the query cache.

topics.title: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR, streaming — how do you choose?
topics.html:
• CSR — empty HTML then JS renders. Fine behind a login. Bad for SEO and for first paint on slow devices.
  • SSG — rendered at build time. Fastest and cheapest. For content that changes on deploy: marketing, docs.
  • ISR — static, regenerated after a revalidation window or on demand. Catalogs, blogs, anything "fresh enough".
  • SSR — rendered per request. Personalised or always-fresh pages; costs server time on every hit.
  • Streaming + Suspense — send the shell immediately, stream slow parts as they resolve. Turns one slow query into a fast page with a skeleton.
  • PPR (Partial Prerendering) — static shell served from the edge, dynamic holes streamed in. The current answer to "static or dynamic?" being a false choice.
// Streaming: the page shell renders instantly, the slow part arrives later
export default function Page() {
  return (
    <>
      <Header />                                {/* instant */}
      <Suspense fallback={<FeedSkeleton />}>
        <Feed />                                {/* awaits a slow query */}
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}
Next 16 note: caching is opt-in now, not aggressive-by-default like Next 14, and route params are async (const { id } = await params). If you quote Next 14 defaults in an interview it dates you.
💬 Say it like this

I choose per route, not for the whole app. Marketing pages are static. A product catalogue is static with revalidation, because data that is one minute old is fine and it is very cheap to serve. A personal dashboard is rendered on every request. And if one section is slow, I put it in a Suspense boundary so the page shell appears immediately and the slow part streams in later. For the user that feels faster than almost any other optimisation.

What's the cost of SSR?
Server CPU and TTFB on every request, plus hydration work on the client. If the page isn't personalised, SSR is usually the wrong tool — static plus revalidation gives the same HTML for a fraction of the cost.
Why did my page become dynamic unexpectedly?
Reading cookies, headers, or searchParams opts a route into dynamic rendering. That's the usual reason a "static" page suddenly hits the server on every request.

topics.title: Server Actions — how they work and how to not make them a security hole.
topics.html:
// app/actions.ts
"use server";
export async function updateProfile(prev: State, formData: FormData): Promise<State> {
  const session = await auth();                       // 1. authenticate — always
  if (!session) return { error: "Unauthorized" };
  const parsed = ProfileSchema.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(formData)); // 2. validate
  if (!parsed.success) return { error: "Invalid input" };
  if (!can(session.user, "edit", parsed.data.id)) return { error: "Forbidden" }; // 3. authorize
  await db.profile.update(parsed.data);
  revalidatePath("/profile");                          // 4. refresh cached data
  return { ok: true };
}

// client
const [state, action, isPending] = useActionState(updateProfile, {});
<form action={action}> ... </form>
  • A Server Action compiles to a public HTTP endpoint. Anyone can call it with any payload — being "only used by my form" is not protection.
  • So every action does the same three things: authenticate, validate the input with a schema, authorize the specific resource. Skipping authorization is the classic RSC-era vulnerability.
  • Pairs with useActionState for pending/error state and useOptimistic for instant UI. Forms still work with JS disabled — progressive enhancement comes free.
  • Not a replacement for a real API when you need REST semantics, third-party consumers, or fine-grained caching.
💬 Say it like this

A server action looks like a normal function call, but underneath it is a POST endpoint that React creates. That is the important mental model: I treat every action like a public API route — check the session, validate the input with Zod, and check that this user is allowed to change this exact record. After that I revalidate the path so the cached data is refreshed.

Where does error handling live?
Return typed error state from the action and render it from useActionState — expected errors are data. Throwing is for unexpected failures, caught by error.tsx.

topics.title: Hydration — what it is, and how do you debug a mismatch?
topics.html:
• Hydration = React walks the server HTML and attaches state and event handlers instead of recreating the DOM. Until it finishes, the page looks interactive but isn't.
  • Mismatch = the client's first render produces different output than the server's. React logs an error and, in the worst case, re-renders the subtree from scratch.
  • Usual causes: Date.now() / Math.random() / new Date().toLocaleString() during render, reading window or localStorage, locale or timezone differences, browser extensions injecting DOM, invalid HTML nesting (<div> inside <p>).
  • Fixes: render the value in useEffect after mount, pass a server-computed value down as a prop, or suppressHydrationWarning for genuinely non-deterministic single values like a timestamp.
  • Perf angle: hydration cost scales with the client bundle — the real fix for slow interactivity is usually less client JS, not faster hydration.
💬 Say it like this

Hydration is React taking the HTML from the server and adding the interactivity to it. A mismatch means the first render in the browser produced different markup. It is almost always something that is not stable between server and client: a date, a random value, or reading localStorage during render. So I look at what React says was different, find the time-, locale- or browser-dependent part, and move it into an effect so it runs only after mount.
